UNDERSTAND THE TWO LAYERS

State law applies in the city, too.

New York City is part of New York State. Applicable state requirements continue to apply in the five boroughs; NYC adds local rules with their own scope.

Selected differences relevant to AI use
ActivityNew York StateAdditional NYC layer
Hiring & promotionThe State Human Rights Law prohibits covered discrimination and requires applicable accommodations.Local Law 144 adds audits and notices for covered hiring tools. The separate City Human Rights Law also matters.
Customer biometricsThe SHIELD Act addresses security of covered private information.Local Law 3 adds entrance signage for covered establishments and restrictions on monetizing biometric information.
Smart building accessRelevant state privacy, security, and housing protections still need to be assessed.Local Law 63 regulates data from covered residential smart-access systems, including biometric entry.
Does NYC’s hiring-tool law apply outside a city office?

DCWP’s guidance includes jobs located in NYC at least part time, fully remote jobs associated with an NYC office, and use by NYC employment agencies. An applicant’s address alone is not the whole scope test.

First check whether the tool meets the AEDT definition and screens applicants for a specific role or employees for promotion. The 10-business-day notice duty concerns NYC-resident candidates and employees.

A bias audit is not a discrimination safe harbor. Other state, city, and federal protections may apply even when Local Law 144 does not.

A GUIDE TO THIS ATLAS

Start with the law.
Follow the source.

This is a curated starting point for AI research, not an exhaustive legal inventory. Coverage includes AI-specific statutes, automated decision-making, synthetic media, and selected privacy and consumer-protection laws relevant to AI. Entries link to primary legal sources or clearly labeled legislative research summaries. New York has an expanded research collection; depth varies by state.

“Enacted” confirms adoption; it does not mean every provision is operative or enforceable. “Upcoming” identifies adopted measures with future duties. “Guidance” identifies agency expectations rather than a newly enacted statute. Amendments, court orders, exceptions, and later developments may affect application. Local measures are labeled separately; proposals are not included in this collection.

The original state survey was checked on 18 September 2026. New York and the additions identified in California and Utah were checked on 22 September 2026. The State/NYC comparison, refreshed NYC hiring entry, and added biometric, tenant-privacy, and civil-rights entries were checked on 26 September 2026. Each entry shows its source-check date. This collection does not update automatically or comprehensively track litigation. General federal, consumer-protection, civil-rights, and sector laws may also apply. Map colors describe the collection, not regulatory strictness.
